topic: The Pi Collision Mystery: How Colliding Blocks Compute Pi
target_audience: High school students with basic physics knowledge and university freshmen

sections.title: The Strange Phenomenon
lecture_lines: Two blocks and a wall create a surprising mystery.
We count every single collision between blocks and walls.
Total collisions magically reveal the digits of Pi.
animations: Create a wall (#FFFFFF) on the left, a small square (m) and a large square (M) on a floor line.
Large square (M) moves toward small square (m) with a velocity vector arrow (#00FF00).
Small square bounces between wall and large square; increment a 'Collisions' counter (#FFFF00).
Text 'Mass Ratio: 1:10,000' appears.
Counter rapidly increases and stops at '314'.

sections.title: Prerequisite 1: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Momentum conservation governs how these blocks bounce.
Energy conservation limits their total possible movement.
Together, these laws define the system's physical state.
animations: Display momentum formula: 'mv + MV = p' (#00BFFF) and energy: '1/2mv^2 + 1/2MV^2 = E' (#FF4500).
Show two blocks colliding with velocity vectors changing size.
Highlight the squared terms in the energy equation.
An ellipse (#FFD700) appears on a v-V plane.
Label the horizontal axis 'v' and vertical axis 'V'.

sections.title: Transforming the Problem into Geometry
lecture_lines: Let's simplify the physics using a clever mathematical trick.
We rescale velocities by the square root of mass.
This transforms the complex energy ellipse into a circle.
Now, every collision is a point on this circle.
The physics problem has become a geometry problem.
animations: Show the energy formula with 'V' being replaced by 'V* = V * sqrt(M)'.
Show the ellipse from Section 2.
Animate the ellipse compressing horizontally into a circle (#ADFF2F).
Label the new vertical axis 'V * sqrt(M)'.
The circle pulses to emphasize the transition.

sections.title: Collisions as Bounces on a Circle
lecture_lines: Each collision moves our point along the circular path.
Block-wall collisions reflect the point across an axis.
Block-block collisions reflect the point across a tilted line.
These reflections bounce the point around the circle's edge.
Counting collisions is like counting bounces inside a mirror.
animations: A circle (#ADFF2F) with a single point (#FF00FF) on its perimeter.
The point 'jumps' to a new location on the circle.
Draw a chord connecting the old point to the new point.
Repeat the jump multiple times, forming a zig-zag path.
Overlay a laser beam effect (#FF0000) on the jumping point.

sections.title: The Arc Length and Pi
lecture_lines: The mass ratio determines the angle of each jump.
Larger masses create smaller angles and more collisions.
Each collision consumes a specific arc of the circle.
The total collisions are limited by the circle's circumference.
This geometric limit is where Pi enters the equation.
animations: Highlight a small arc (#FFA500) on the circle from Section 4.
Label the arc angle as 'theta'.
Show that smaller theta means more segments fit in the circle.
Animate a clock-like hand sweeping the circle in discrete steps.
Display '2pi / theta' near the circle.

sections.title: The Grand Reveal
lecture_lines: As mass increases, collision counts match Pi more closely.
Geometry explains why these digits appear in our world.
Physics and Pi are connected through this simple setup.
animations: Fade in four small circles (#FFFFFF).
Each circle fills with collision paths of different densities.
Counters below them stop at: 3, 31, 314, 3141.
The digits of Pi (#FFFF00) glow and move to the center.
